modalities.name: The Relief Shift
modalities.tagline: Ideal parents take over the jobs your protective habits still do.
modalities.whatItIs: The Relief Shift is a new concept for imagery-based therapy that sees each protective habit, such as constant worry, people-pleasing or staying busy, as a job a child took on because some kind of care was missing. It pairs getting to know that protective part with imagining ideal parent figures who do the job instead. The protector is never pushed aside: it watches and decides for itself whether it can rest.
modalities.coreIdea: A protective habit may still be doing a job a caregiver should have done, like staying on guard or making sure nobody gets upset. When imagined ideal parents visibly take over that exact job, the part that has been on duty since childhood may finally come off shift.
modalities.whatYouDo: In 60-minute one-to-one sessions, a licensed clinician trained in trauma care helps you turn inward, find a protective habit and ask it what it guards against and what care was missing when it started. You then imagine being a young child with ideal parent figures, never your real parents, who do that job for you, for example keeping watch so you can play, while the protective part looks on. Each session ends by asking the protector how the scene felt to it, and the scene is repeated over several weeks with a recording for home practice.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who notice protective patterns that started early, such as constant vigilance or harsh self-criticism, and want to work on their roots with a therapist. It may suit people who are drawn to both parts work and imagery.
modalities.cautions: This is an untested blend of two lightly researched methods, and imagining childhood care can bring up painful memories or a strong backlash from protective parts, so a licensed clinician trained in trauma care leads every session, and it should not replace well-tested care for PTSD, depression or a crisis. The childhood scenes are imagined, not recalled: it uses only memories you already have, treats images and feelings as experiences rather than evidence of what happened, and is never used to uncover forgotten events.
modalities.tweet: New concept: The Relief Shift. Your worrying or people-pleasing may be doing a job a parent should have done. In guided imagery with a therapist, ideal parent figures take over that job, so the part of you on duty since childhood might finally rest.

modalities.name: Kindly Taught Skills
modalities.tagline: Learn coping skills as if taught by the parents you needed.
modalities.whatItIs: Kindly Taught Skills is a new concept for structured, skills-based therapy in which each practical skill, such as naming a feeling, catching a worried thought or breaking a fear into small steps, is first learned in imagery from ideal parent figures. You picture yourself as a child while patient, warm parents teach you the skill, then practice the same skill on a real, current problem with worksheets and homework. It never goes looking for forgotten events: it works only with what you already remember, and any image or feeling that comes up is treated as part of the exercise, not as evidence of the past.
modalities.coreIdea: Many adults never had anyone calmly show them how to handle a feeling, so coping skills learned later can feel cold and borrowed. Learning each skill first from imagined ideal parents, then practicing it in daily life, aims to make the skills feel like your own and to tie them to a sense of being cared for.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over about 10 weekly sessions with a therapist trained in both cognitive behavioral methods and attachment work, each session covers one skill. The therapist first guides a 10-minute scene in which ideal parent figures teach you that skill as a child, kindly and step by step, and you then apply it to a present-day problem using a short worksheet. Between sessions you practice the skill daily, log how it went and bring the log to the next session.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want the structure and practical tools of cognitive behavioral work but find that skills taught in a textbook way never quite stick. It may suit those who grew up without anyone who coached them through hard feelings.
modalities.cautions: Untested: scenes of being taught and cared for as a child can stir grief or painful memories, so the therapist should be trained in trauma care and ready to slow down. This concept is no replacement for established therapy for depression or anxiety, and anyone with suicidal thoughts needs prompt professional help.
modalities.tweet: An idea: Kindly Taught Skills. Each coping skill (naming a feeling, checking a worry, facing a fear in small steps) is first learned in guided imagery from patient ideal parents, then practiced on real problems. Skills that feel given, not borrowed.

modalities.name: The Lit-Up List
modalities.tagline: Find your values in what imagined, attentive parents saw you love.
modalities.whatItIs: The Lit-Up List is an untested way to look for what matters to you by imagining ideal parent figures who noticed, and delighted in, whatever made you light up as a child. The delights they point out become a list of values, and each week you take one small step toward one of them, making room for any fear that comes along. Nothing here is meant to uncover forgotten events: only memories you already hold are used, and pictures or feelings that arise are not proof of what really happened.
modalities.coreIdea: Values are easier to find when someone attuned helps you look, and easier to act on with a secure base behind you. Imagined ideal parents can play both roles, noticing what you love and cheering you toward it while you carry your nerves with you.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 50-minute session, a therapist guides a short scene in which ideal parent figures watch you as a child at play and say aloud what they see you loving, such as building things, helping or making people laugh. You write these down as your list, link one item to a small action for the coming week, and practice letting fear or doubt ride along instead of waiting for it to pass. The next session begins by reviewing the step and what helped or got in the way.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel cut off from what they want, or who know their values but freeze when it is time to act on them. It may suit those who find standard values worksheets too abstract.
modalities.cautions: Nobody has tested this yet, and imagining an attentive childhood can bring up grief for what was missing, so it is best done with a therapist who works with attachment and can pace the imagery. It is meant for personal growth and is not a replacement for tested care for depression or other conditions.
modalities.tweet: What if your values are hiding in what you loved as a kid? The Lit-Up List is a new idea: guided imagery of ideal parents who notice what lights you up, then one small step a week toward it, nerves and all. A gentle way back to what you want.

modalities.name: Off-Script Parents
modalities.tagline: Ideal parents contradict the one old lesson behind a stubborn symptom.
modalities.whatItIs: Off-Script Parents is a proposed experiential therapy that starts from a stubborn symptom and looks for the hidden emotional lesson that makes it feel necessary, such as "if I need anything, I will be left". Once that lesson is found and felt, ideal parent figures are imagined going off the lesson's script, doing exactly what it says can never happen, while you still feel the old lesson. The scenes are an imagined childhood, not a rewrite of what really happened: the work uses only memories you already have, treats images and feelings as experiences rather than evidence, and is never used to uncover forgotten events.
modalities.coreIdea: Some symptoms may persist because a lesson learned early still makes them feel necessary. Feeling that lesson and, at the same moment, a vivid imagined experience that plainly contradicts it may give the old learning a chance to update.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over roughly 8 to 12 sessions led by a licensed clinician trained in trauma care, you first explore a symptom until you can feel and put into words the lesson behind it, as the child who learned it might say it. The clinician then builds an ideal-parent scene tailored to that one lesson, for example parents who move closer the moment you need them, and guides you to hold the old feeling and the new scene together. The scene is repeated over several sessions, with a recording for home use, while you note in a simple diary whether the old pattern still shows up in daily life.
modalities.whoItsFor: People with one specific, persistent pattern, such as panic when someone gets close or a refusal ever to ask for help, who want to understand why it keeps happening. It suits those comfortable with emotionally vivid work in session.
modalities.cautions: An untested concept: uncovering and contradicting old emotional lessons can be intense, so a licensed clinician trained in trauma care must lead it, and medical causes of a symptom should be ruled out first. It should not replace well-tested care for conditions such as major depression or PTSD.
modalities.tweet: Thought experiment: what if a stubborn habit stays loyal to a lesson you learned as a child? Off-Script Parents finds that one lesson, then a therapist guides imagery of ideal parents doing exactly what the lesson says can't happen. Untested, deep work.

modalities.name: Let Go Under Guard
modalities.tagline: Feel protected first, then let the body shake out tension.
modalities.whatItIs: Let Go Under Guard is an untried pairing of gentle, self-paced body tremoring with imagery of protective ideal parent figures. It builds a felt sense of being guarded before the shaking starts, keeps the figures standing watch throughout, and returns to that protection whenever the tremors feel like too much. Only memories you already have are used, vivid images and feelings are not taken as evidence of what happened, and the practice is never used to uncover forgotten events.
modalities.coreIdea: The guiding hunch is that a body lets go of tension more easily when it feels guarded. Imagined protectors supply the guarding, and the mild tremors happen inside that felt shelter rather than while you feel exposed.
modalities.whatYouDo: You learn it over four to six sessions with a clinician who is also a trained tremoring (TRE) provider and who first screens your physical and mental health: 10 minutes of imagery in which ideal parent figures stand guard around you, a few simple leg-tiring stretches, then lying on your back with knees bent and letting mild tremors run while you keep sensing the figures nearby. Each round lasts a few minutes at most, you can end it at any moment by straightening your legs or rolling onto your side, and every session ends with rest in the protective scene. Only after that do you practice at home, about twice a week for up to 30 minutes, with a recording of the imagery and regular check-ins with the same clinician.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who carry a lot of physical tension and find talking about the past hard, but who feel too unguarded to let their body relax. It may suit those who respond to both imagery and body-based practice.
modalities.cautions: Untested: tremoring and childhood imagery can each bring up strong emotions or memories, so anyone with severe trauma, dissociation, psychosis or bipolar disorder should do it only with a clinically trained provider alongside their own care, and anyone with epilepsy or seizures, pregnancy, recent surgery, fractures or other injuries should check with a doctor first. Stop whenever you feel overwhelmed, numb or in pain, and use it alongside other care, never instead of it.
modalities.tweet: Untested idea: Let Go Under Guard. The hunch: some bodies only let go of tension once they feel guarded. After a health screening, a clinician guides imagery of protective figures standing watch while gentle tremors run. You can end any round at once.

modalities.name: Parents That Fit
modalities.tagline: Your body's felt sense designs the parent figures it needs.
modalities.whatItIs: Parents That Fit is a proposed practice in which a vague bodily felt sense, rather than a standard script, decides what imagined ideal parent figures should be like. You check each detail of the imagined parents against that inner sense, adjusting their voice, closeness or manner until something in the body eases. It does not dig for forgotten events, it stays with memories you already have, and whatever images or feelings arise are not treated as evidence about the past.
modalities.coreIdea: A standard picture of a good parent rarely fits everyone, and the body may sense what kind of care it missed before words do. Letting the felt sense shape the figures, and checking each change for a small felt shift, aims to make the imagined care feel truly your own.
modalities.whatYouDo: In 45-minute sessions with a therapist trained in Focusing and attachment work, you sit quietly, notice the felt sense of an old longing and ask it what a parent would need to be like for it. Each word or image that comes, such as "someone slow, who sits beside me rather than across from me", is added to the scene and checked against the body for fit. Once the figures feel right, usually after several sessions, the therapist records a short version for brief home practice and stays available to talk.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who found generic comforting imagery hollow, or who sense things more easily in the body than in pictures. It suits those who want a gentle, slow way to explore early longings.
modalities.cautions: An untested idea: turning toward early longings can bring up grief or painful memories, so the therapist should be trained in trauma care and home practice should wait until the work feels steady. It is not a substitute for tested care for depression or other conditions.
modalities.tweet: Does generic comforting imagery leave you cold? Parents That Fit is a new concept: with a therapist, let a vague feeling in your body shape imagined ideal parents, adjusting them until something inside eases. Care designed by your own body, not a script.

modalities.name: Seen Without a Plan
modalities.tagline: Imagined parents who see you as already whole, not a project.
modalities.whatItIs: Seen Without a Plan is a speculative form of presence-based coaching built around imagined ideal parent figures who see you as complete and have no plan to improve you. They regard you the way a parent might watch a child absorbed in play, wanting nothing changed, and the guide helps you notice in the body what it is like to be seen that way. The childhood scenes are imagined, not recalled: it uses only memories you already have, treats images and feelings as experiences rather than evidence of what happened, and is never used to uncover forgotten events.
modalities.coreIdea: Much self-help, and even much loving care, carries a quiet message that you should become better first. Feeling regarded with no plan for your improvement may ease the pressure to earn your place, leaving room for change that comes without being pushed.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 60-minute one-to-one session, a licensed clinician trained in trauma care, working in an unhurried coaching style, leads a slow scene in which you, as a child, are simply looked at with warm regard by ideal parent figures, without praise for achievements or plans for your future. The guide watches for small changes in your breath, posture and voice and names them gently, while you put into words whatever the regard stirs. Sessions run weekly for about three months, and many end with a few quiet minutes of simply being seen.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel like a permanent self-improvement project, or who felt loved mainly for what they achieved. It suits those drawn to slow, contemplative work who are not in crisis.
modalities.cautions: Untested and deep: being seen without demands can stir grief about your real childhood, which is why a licensed clinician trained in trauma care leads it rather than a coach alone. People in crisis, or with severe depression, PTSD, psychosis or suicidal thoughts, should put established treatment first.
modalities.tweet: Ever feel like a permanent self-improvement project? Seen Without a Plan is a concept: a trauma-trained clinician guides imagery of ideal parents who look at you with warm regard and no plan to improve you. No goals, no fixing, just being seen as whole.

modalities.name: Nothing Asked of You
modalities.tagline: Sit and do nothing while kind imagined parents simply stay nearby.
modalities.whatItIs: Nothing Asked of You is a proposed meditation in which you do nothing at all while sensing that kind, ideal parent figures are quietly nearby, wanting nothing from you. They do not guide, soothe or teach; they are simply there, the way a calm parent might read in a chair while a child plays or daydreams. The past enters only through memories you already have; imagery and feelings are never treated as evidence of what happened, and the practice is never used to uncover forgotten events.
modalities.coreIdea: Many people cannot stop striving, even in meditation, perhaps because part of them still expects to be judged on how well they do. Sensing imagined parents who want nothing from you may make it easier to drop every effort, including the effort to meditate well.
modalities.whatYouDo: A therapist who also teaches meditation introduces it over two or three sessions and records a short guided opening for you. At home you then sit or lie comfortably for 15 to 25 minutes, briefly picture ideal parent figures settling somewhere nearby, then let go of the picture and of any intention to steer your attention, allowing whatever happens (drifting, daydreaming or restlessness) and letting go even of trying to do it right. The therapist stays available to talk about anything that comes up.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel guilty or anxious whenever they are not being productive, and people who find meditation effortful and strained. It may especially suit people who rarely felt allowed to just be as children.
modalities.cautions: Since this is only a concept, go gently: picturing kind parent figures can stir grief about your real childhood, and open sitting with so little structure can bring up worry, old memories or other difficult experiences, so keep sessions short at first and stop if it feels bad. People with significant trauma, dissociation or depression should go slowly with the therapist's support and avoid long or intensive sits.
modalities.tweet: Proposal for anyone who can't rest without feeling guilty: Nothing Asked of You. Sit for 20 minutes, sense kind imagined parents nearby who want nothing from you, and do nothing at all. Daydreaming allowed. An untested twist on open meditation.

modalities.name: Full Cup Goodwill
modalities.tagline: Receive kindness from imagined parents first, then let it overflow.
modalities.whatItIs: Full Cup Goodwill reimagines loving-kindness meditation so that it begins by receiving rather than sending. You first imagine ideal parent figures silently wishing you well, let that warm feeling grow until your attention rests in it, and only then pass goodwill outward in a widening circle.
modalities.coreIdea: Many people struggle to wish themselves well, perhaps because they never felt freely wished well. Filling up on imagined goodwill first may give the outward wishes a real source instead of a strained effort.
modalities.whatYouDo: You learn it over about four sessions with a therapist who also teaches meditation, then practice daily at home with a recording of their voice and check in with them every few weeks. In each 30-minute sit you spend about 10 minutes imagining ideal parent figures offering you, as a child, phrases such as "may you be happy, may you be safe", resting on the warmth this brings and letting it grow without grasping. When it feels full, you pass the same phrases on to a loved one, a neutral person, someone difficult and finally everyone.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find loving-kindness practice dry, forced or upsetting when it starts with themselves. It suits those who want more warmth in daily life and like a clear, repeatable routine.
modalities.cautions: An untested idea: receiving imagined kindness can stir grief, anger or a sense of unworthiness, so start with short sessions and stop if it becomes overwhelming. People with significant trauma, or a history of psychosis, mania or dissociation, should talk to a clinician first and learn deeper absorption only with an experienced teacher.
modalities.tweet: Struggle to wish yourself well? Here's a new idea: Full Cup Goodwill. First imagine kind parent figures wishing you happiness and let that warmth build. Only when you feel full do you send it out to others. Kindness meditation that starts by receiving. 🌱

modalities.name: Lighthouse Body Sweep
modalities.tagline: Scan the body with the steady, warm attention of an ideal parent.
modalities.whatItIs: The Lighthouse Body Sweep is a hypothetical insight meditation in which you move attention slowly through the body while giving that attention the qualities of an ideal parent: steady, warm and unbothered by storms. You note each sensation and watch it change, as in insight practice, but the watching itself is meant to feel like being calmly looked after. Any memories involved are ones you already have, nothing is done to uncover forgotten events, and images or feelings that surface are not evidence of what happened.
modalities.coreIdea: Children may learn to bear strong feelings partly by being met by a caregiver who stays steady. Here the steadiness of close, non-reacting observation is joined with that kind of care, so that even-mindedness can feel protective rather than cold.
modalities.whatYouDo: It is taught over a few small-group sessions co-led by a meditation teacher and a therapist, who open with a brief image of ideal parent figures keeping calm watch. You then sit for 30 to 45 minutes, moving attention section by section from head to feet, noting sensations such as pressure, warmth or tightness and keeping the beam steady through unpleasant ones, the way a calm parent stays put through a child's storm. Daily home practice with a recording follows, with regular check-ins with the same teachers.
modalities.whoItsFor: People drawn to insight meditation who find that close self-observation turns harsh or clinical. It may also suit those who want a structured, well-mapped sitting practice with a warmer tone.
modalities.cautions: Not yet studied: the parent imagery can stir grief about your real childhood, and long sitting can bring up fear, panic, old memories or unusual states, so build up gradually with the therapist's support. People with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or a current crisis should talk to a clinician before longer sits or retreats.
modalities.tweet: Speculative practice: the Lighthouse Body Sweep. If watching yourself in meditation feels cold or harsh, scan your body slowly with the steady, warm attention of an ideal parent who isn't rattled by storms. Observation meant to feel like being looked after.

modalities.name: Comfort Comes After
modalities.tagline: Hard bursts of effort, each followed by imagined comfort from ideal parents.
modalities.whatItIs: Comfort Comes After is a new concept for interval training in which every bout of hard work is followed by a recovery period spent receiving imagined comfort from ideal parent figures. Effort and comfort alternate on a timer, so the body gets repeated practice in a simple sequence: strain, then care. Images and feelings that come up are treated as experiences, not as evidence of what happened; it works with memories you already have and never tries to uncover forgotten ones.
modalities.coreIdea: Part of secure attachment is the learned expectation that distress will be followed by comfort. Interval training already alternates strain and recovery, so spending each recovery feeling soothed may rehearse that expectation in the body.
modalities.whatYouDo: A therapist trained in attachment work meets you for a first session, helps you shape the comfort scene and records it, and a coach sets up the exercise side. Then, two or three times a week on a stationary bike, you warm up for 10 minutes and do 6 to 8 bouts of 1 minute at a hard but manageable effort, each followed by 2 minutes of easy pedaling while the recording guides you to imagine ideal parent figures soothing and encouraging you. A cool-down ends with a short rest in the scene, and the therapist stays available to talk about anything it stirs.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like vigorous exercise but tend to meet their own struggles with harshness, and who want a short, structured routine. It may appeal to those who find imagery easier to feel when their body is activated.
modalities.cautions: Untested: hard bouts put a heavy load on the heart, so check with a doctor before starting (especially with heart problems, fainting or high blood pressure), always warm up, build up gradually and stop at once for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. The imagery belongs only to the easy recovery on a stationary bike, and because imagined comfort can stir grief about your real childhood, bring anything strong that surfaces to the therapist.
modalities.tweet: Workout concept: Comfort Comes After. One minute of hard pedaling, then two easy minutes imagining kind parent figures soothing you. Repeat. The idea is to train your body to expect that hard moments are followed by care. Doctor check first. 🚲

modalities.name: Picked With a Reason
modalities.tagline: A team game built so every player feels wanted, protected and cheered.
modalities.whatItIs: Picked With a Reason is an untried group format that uses a light, cooperative team game to offer a lived taste of secure belonging, framed by short imagery of ideal parent figures watching from the sideline. Its rules make sure every player is chosen with a reason, looked after by a partner and cheered for trying as much as for succeeding. The sideline figures are imagined and nothing in the session asks you to recall the past: it uses only memories you already have, treats images and feelings as experiences rather than evidence of what happened, and is never used to uncover forgotten events.
modalities.coreIdea: Many adults carry memories of being picked last, teased or left on the sidelines. Pairing a game built around being wanted, protected and encouraged with imagined parents who are glad to watch aims to give a fresh experience of belonging, felt both in the body and in imagination.
modalities.whatYouDo: A coach trained in trauma-aware group work leads a weekly 90-minute session for 8 to 14 adults over six weeks, with a therapist co-leading the first and last sessions and available in between; after a warm-up jog and stretches, a 5-minute guided image invites you to picture ideal parent figures settling on the sideline, glad to watch you play as you are now, and each player then invites another onto their team with one reason why. Teams play a gentle, low-contact disc or ball game at a moderate pace on flat, even grass, in buddy pairs who check on each other, every attempt gets a cheer, and at water breaks players briefly look back to their imagined sideline. The session ends in a circle where players say what it felt like to be wanted today, keeping to the present rather than the past.
modalities.whoItsFor: Adults who avoid group sport because of old experiences of exclusion or criticism, and anyone who wants to feel what belonging can be like. It suits people who enjoy light play more than competition.
modalities.cautions: Untested: running and quick turns carry some risk of strains and falls, so check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems, warm up, keep the pace moderate and stop at once for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. The imagery can still stir memories of exclusion or of your real childhood, so anyone strongly stirred can step out, and the therapist can suggest individual support.
modalities.tweet: Picked last in gym class? Picked With a Reason is a team game invented with you in mind: each player is asked onto a team and told why, has a buddy, gets cheered for every try, and pictures kind parent figures glad to watch from the sideline.

modalities.name: Still Beside You
modalities.tagline: An easy run or walk beside an imagined companion who stays.
modalities.whatItIs: Still Beside You is a new concept that joins steady endurance exercise with imagery of an ideal parent figure who moves alongside you for the whole session. The point is constancy: minute after minute, you notice that the imagined companion is still there, matching your rhythm without pushing ahead or dropping back. It never goes looking for forgotten events: it works only with what you already remember, and any image or feeling that comes up is treated as part of the exercise, not as evidence of the past.
modalities.coreIdea: A sense of security may grow from care that stays reliable over time, not only from single warm moments. Long, rhythmic movement gives that reliability something to be felt in, since every stride is another moment in which someone is still with you.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two or three times a week you go for a 30 to 45 minute easy jog or brisk walk on a familiar, safe route in daylight, starting with five minutes of easy walking and keeping to a pace where you can still talk. A recorded guide made with a clinician checks in every few minutes, inviting you to sense the ideal parent figure beside you, matching your pace, and to notice that they have not left. You finish by walking slowly and naming one moment when the company felt real.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who fear being left or find it hard to trust that care will last, and who already enjoy, or want to start, steady running or walking. It may suit those who prefer a practice they can do alone with a recording.
modalities.cautions: An untested idea: check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems, build up time and distance slowly to avoid common running injuries, stop at once for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and keep your attention on traffic, terrain and weather, skipping icy or very hot days. Feelings about being left can surface, so a therapist familiar with attachment work should help shape the recording and be available to talk.
modalities.tweet: Here's an experimental one for runners and walkers: Still Beside You. On an easy jog, a recorded guide invites you to sense an imagined ideal parent beside you, matching your rhythm, never dropping back. Practice in trusting that care can last.

modalities.name: Doorframe Marks
modalities.tagline: Strength training where imagined parents proudly mark every gain.
modalities.whatItIs: Doorframe Marks is an idea for pairing a simple, progressive strength routine with imagery of ideal parent figures who notice and take pride in each small gain, the way some parents pencil a child's height on a doorframe. Your training log becomes that doorframe: a visible record of growth that is witnessed, not just counted. Nothing here is meant to uncover forgotten events: only memories you already hold are used, and pictures or feelings that arise are not proof of what really happened.
modalities.coreIdea: Getting measurably stronger gives concrete proof that effort pays off, and encouragement from someone who delights in your growth is one of the qualities linked with secure attachment. Joining the two aims to let progress feel not only earned but warmly seen.
modalities.whatYouDo: A coach teaches you good form over a few sessions, and a therapist trained in attachment work meets you at the start to shape the imagery and record a short weekly scene. You then train twice a week in a gym or at home: after a 5 to 10 minute warm-up, 5 or 6 basic exercises such as squats, rows and presses, 2 to 3 sets of 8 to 12 controlled repetitions at a moderate weight, adding weight or repetitions gradually, logging every session and, between sets, imagining ideal parent figures watching with quiet pride. Once a week you look back over your log with the recorded scene, and the therapist stays available to talk about anything it stirs.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who grew up with little encouragement, or whose efforts went unnoticed, and who like clear goals and visible progress. It suits beginners as well as experienced lifters.
modalities.cautions: Untested so far: check with a doctor first if you have high blood pressure, heart problems or serious eye disease, warm up, learn good technique, add weight gradually, avoid holding your breath while lifting and stop at once for chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. If the focus slides toward appearance or comparison, or old feelings of never being good enough surface strongly, pause the imagery and talk it through with the therapist.
modalities.tweet: Concept sketch: Doorframe Marks. Remember pencil marks of a kid's height on a doorframe? Your lifting log becomes the doorframe: you train steadily and imagine ideal parents proudly noticing each gain. Progress that is witnessed, not just counted. 💪

modalities.name: The Glad Greeting
modalities.tagline: A dog's real gladness becomes the model for imagined parental delight.
modalities.whatItIs: The Glad Greeting is a proposed form of animal-assisted therapy in which a trained dog's obvious pleasure at seeing you becomes a living example of being delighted in. A therapist helps you take in that real, uncomplicated welcome, then guides you to imagine ideal parent figures greeting you as a child with the same gladness. Only memories you already have are used, vivid images and feelings are not taken as evidence of what happened, and the practice is never used to uncover forgotten events.
modalities.coreIdea: Delight is one of the qualities linked with secure attachment, yet some people have little felt memory of being greeted with it. A friendly animal offers a real, present example that the imagination can borrow, which may make imagined delight easier to feel.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 50-minute session, you enter a quiet room where a therapist and a trained therapy dog with its handler are waiting, and you notice, slowly, how the dog greets you and settles near you. You then sit with the dog for as long as it chooses to stay (it is always free to wander off or rest), perhaps with a hand on its back, while the therapist guides a short scene of ideal parents greeting you the same way. Each session ends with talking about what it was like to be welcomed, and sessions repeat weekly for a few months.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel unwelcome or like a burden, and who relax around animals. It may especially suit those for whom imagined care feels fake until they have felt a real example.
modalities.cautions: Untested: check for allergies and fear of dogs, never force contact, and choose a licensed therapist working with a trained animal team that follows animal welfare guidelines, limits the dog's workload and lets it leave or rest whenever it wants. Imagery about childhood can bring up grief or memories, so the therapist should be trained in trauma care.
modalities.tweet: Imagine a friendly dog greeting you, all wagging gladness. The Glad Greeting is an idea for animal-assisted therapy: a therapist helps you take in that real welcome, then imagine ideal parents greeting you the same way. A welcome felt before it is imagined. 🐕

modalities.name: Five Gestures of Care
modalities.tagline: A slow movement form where each gesture gives one kind of care.
modalities.whatItIs: Five Gestures of Care is an invented movement practice: a short, slow sequence of five gestures, each embodying one quality linked with secure attachment and offered to yourself. Like a qigong form, it coordinates slow movement with breath and calm attention, but each gesture is paired with the feeling of receiving that quality from an imagined ideal parent. It does not dig for forgotten events, it stays with memories you already have, and whatever images or feelings arise are not treated as evidence about the past.
modalities.coreIdea: Care is first known through the body, through being held, rocked and looked at, so it may be easier to rebuild through movement than through words. Repeating a simple form in which the body acts out protection, comfort, attention, encouragement and delight aims to make those qualities physically familiar.
modalities.whatYouDo: Standing or seated, you move through five gestures over about 15 minutes, repeating each slowly with the breath: arms arching overhead like a shelter for protection, hands resting on the chest for comfort, palms opening at eye level for being seen, arms sweeping forward for encouragement and hands lifting upward for delight, while imagining an ideal parent offering each quality. The form is learned over about six small-group classes co-led by a qigong teacher and a therapist trained in attachment work. Home practice comes after that, with a recording and monthly check-ins with the therapist.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want to work on feeling cared for but find sitting imagery hard, and those who prefer gentle movement to talking. It may suit older adults or people with limited fitness, since every gesture can be done seated.
modalities.cautions: The form has never been tried or studied, and while the movements are gentle, adapt them to your body and know that receiving imagined care can stir grief or old memories. People with significant trauma or a history of psychosis should talk to their own clinician before starting, and anyone can pause the imagery and simply move.
modalities.tweet: Brand-new idea: Five Gestures of Care. A slow, qigong-like sequence where each movement offers you one quality of good parenting: shelter, comfort, being seen, encouragement and delight. Meant to let you feel cared for through the body, not just words.

modalities.name: Care You Already Have
modalities.tagline: From ideal imagined parents to real people who are good enough.
modalities.whatItIs: Care You Already Have is a new concept that takes the qualities found in ideal-parent imagery, such as protection, comfort, attention, encouragement and delight, and uses them as a guide for real social life. You map which people already offer you small versions of each, spend deliberate time with them, and practice letting those moments land. The past enters only through memories you already have; imagery and feelings are never treated as evidence of what happened, and the practice is never used to uncover forgotten events.
modalities.coreIdea: Imagined ideal parents can show what good care feels like, but lasting security is lived among real people who are imperfect yet good enough. Noticing and taking in real moments of care may help a new sense of security take root in daily life.
modalities.whatYouDo: In one or two opening sessions, a counselor or therapist helps you draw a simple map of friends, relatives, mentors and neighbors and note which quality each tends to offer, such as the friend who delights in your news. Each week you then plan two or three contacts with these people, from a call to a shared meal, and afterwards spend a minute recalling the moment of care and letting it sink in. You also notice when you pull away and try one small step toward someone instead, reviewing it all with the counselor every few weeks.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who have done inner work on early relationships and want it to show up in everyday life, and anyone who feels lonely despite knowing people. It suits those who like a light plan rather than strict rules.
modalities.cautions: An untested idea: favor people who feel safe, step back from anyone hostile, controlling or abusive, and expect that mapping who cares for you can stir grief about care that was missing early on, which is worth bringing to the counselor. If social situations bring intense fear, or low mood persists, talk to a doctor or therapist, since this may be social anxiety or depression, for which well-tested help exists.
modalities.tweet: Lonely among acquaintances? A novel practice: Care You Already Have. Map who already gives you comfort, encouragement or delight, plan time with them each week, and let those moments sink in. Real, imperfect people rather than ideal imagined ones.

modalities.name: The Waiting Bench
modalities.tagline: Explore outdoors in loops from a spot where imagined parents wait.
modalities.whatItIs: The Waiting Bench, an untried nature practice, turns a slow walk into loops of exploring and coming back. You choose a home spot, ideally a bench, imagine ideal parent figures waiting there, then wander off with curiosity and return to be welcomed, in loops that grow a little longer each time. Any memories involved are ones you already have, nothing is done to uncover forgotten events, and images or feelings that surface are not evidence of what happened.
modalities.coreIdea: Securely attached children tend to explore boldly because they know a welcome is waiting when they come back. Acting out that rhythm in a real landscape aims to let curiosity and comfort be felt together rather than as opposites.
modalities.whatYouDo: The first walk is led by a therapist trained in attachment work, who helps you choose the bench and shape the welcoming imagery; after that you walk alone or in a small group, with the therapist available to talk. In a park or quiet woodland you walk for 45 to 60 minutes in three to five loops from the bench, starting with a few minutes away and building up to fifteen or twenty. While away you follow whatever catches your senses (a sound, a path, a patch of light), and on each return you pause at the bench and imagine being warmly received before setting off again.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who hold on tight to others or find it hard to venture out, and anyone who wants a nature walk with a gentle emotional purpose. It suits most fitness levels.
modalities.cautions: An untested concept: choose familiar, safe routes, check the weather, carry water and tell someone where you are, so the loops never risk getting you lost. If the imagery stirs strong sadness about your real childhood, bring it to the therapist before walking on alone.
modalities.tweet: Idea for your next walk: The Waiting Bench. Pick a bench as home base, imagine kind parent figures waiting there, then wander off and come back to be welcomed, in ever longer loops. Exploring, with a welcome to return to. 🌳 #NatureWalk

modalities.name: The Blanket Bridge
modalities.tagline: Real comforting sensations lend life to imagined care.
modalities.whatItIs: The Blanket Bridge is a new concept that uses real, present comfort for the senses, such as the weight of a blanket, the heat of a mug or a soft familiar smell, to make imagined care feel more vivid. You attend slowly and mindfully to each sensation and let imagery of being looked after by ideal parent figures attach itself to it. Images and feelings that come up are treated as experiences, not as evidence of what happened; it works with memories you already have and never tries to uncover forgotten ones.
modalities.coreIdea: Imagined care can feel thin to people who rely on what they can sense, while plain sensations can feel empty of meaning. Joining the two lets real sensations act as a bridge to imagined care, so that later the blanket or mug alone may bring back a feeling of being safe.
modalities.whatYouDo: A therapist trained in attachment work guides the first two or three sessions and records a version for you to use at home. Each 20-minute session starts with wrapping yourself in a warm blanket and holding a warm drink, exploring each sensation with slow, curious attention and, when one feels comforting, imagining it as part of being cared for as a child by ideal parents before returning to plain sensing. You then practice at home with the recording, the therapist stays available to talk, and the hope is that after a few weeks the blanket or drink alone serves as a reminder.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose mental pictures feel faint but who respond strongly to touch, warmth and sound, and anyone who wants a soothing evening routine. It may suit those already working with a therapist on early relationships.
modalities.cautions: Untested: imagining being cared for as a child can bring up painful memories of your real childhood, and some sensations, smells or sounds can unexpectedly do the same, so people with significant trauma should go at the therapist's pace and anyone can stop at any time. It is a self-care idea, not a stand-alone answer to severe anxiety, PTSD or depression.
modalities.tweet: If pictures in your mind feel faint but your senses feel everything, a new idea: the Blanket Bridge. Wrap up in a blanket, hold a warm mug, notice each sensation slowly, and let those real comforts make imagined care from ideal parents feel more vivid.

modalities.name: The Song You Needed
modalities.tagline: Write and record the song ideal parents would have sung you.
modalities.whatItIs: The Song You Needed is a proposed music therapy approach in which you write, with a music therapist, the song that ideal parent figures would have sung to you as a child. The lyrics put the qualities of secure care into your own words, and a simple recording becomes something you can return to at home. The parents in the song are imagined, not recalled: it uses only memories you already have, treats images and feelings as experiences rather than evidence of what happened, and is never used to uncover forgotten events.
modalities.coreIdea: For many people music carries feeling in ways words alone cannot, and a voice singing to you is one of the oldest forms of comfort. A personal song in the voice of the parents you needed may make imagined care easier to feel and easier to come back to.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over about six weekly sessions with a credentialed music therapist, you imagine ideal parents and listen for what they would want you to know, then shape those phrases into a short song in any style you like, from a lullaby to a folk tune. The therapist helps with melody and recording, sung by you or by the therapist. You then listen to the recording a few times a week at a gentle volume, and talk in session about what it stirs.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who respond strongly to music or find it hard to put feelings into words, and who want to explore early longings in a creative way. No musical skill is needed.
modalities.cautions: Still only an idea: hearing tender words sung to you can bring up grief, so work with a credentialed music therapist with trauma training, and notice if listening starts to deepen a low mood. It is an add-on to, not a replacement for, professional care for serious depression or other mental illness.
modalities.tweet: A hypothetical practice for music lovers: The Song You Needed. With a music therapist, you write the song ideal parents would have sung to you as a child, record it, and play it at home. Comfort in a voice and tune you can replay. 🎵

modalities.name: Co-Signed Experiments
modalities.tagline: Find the part behind a hot thought, then test its fear together.
modalities.whatItIs: Co-Signed Experiments is a speculative blend of the worksheets and real-life experiments of cognitive behavioral work with the view that the mind is made of parts. Each upsetting automatic thought is traced to the part that says it, its fear is heard with curiosity, and any experiment to test that fear is designed only with the part's agreement. It stays with present-day situations: it uses only memories you already have, treats images and feelings as experiences rather than evidence of the past, and is never used to uncover forgotten events.
modalities.coreIdea: Behavioral experiments can stall when one side of a person quietly vetoes them. If the part that predicts disaster helps design the test and agrees to watch the result, the experiment may be both kinder and more likely to happen.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over 10 to 12 weekly sessions, you keep a thought record with two extra columns: which part seems to be speaking, and what it fears would happen. In session, a therapist helps you ask that part what small test it could tolerate, such as speaking up once in a meeting, and what it wants to watch for. After each experiment you write down what actually happened and report back to the part, in your own words, before planning the next step.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like structure and homework but feel torn inside, or who notice that one side of them keeps blocking plans to face their fears. It suits those who want present-focused change that respects their inner conflicts.
modalities.cautions: An untested idea: experiments mean facing anxious situations in small steps, and turning toward parts can sometimes bring up old pain, so work with a therapist trained in both approaches. People with severe trauma, dissociation or a current crisis need a licensed clinician and well-tested care first.
modalities.tweet: For anyone whose inner critic vetoes every plan, a new concept: Co-Signed Experiments. When a thought like 'they'll laugh at me' shows up, ask which part of you is saying it and what it fears, then design a small real-world test that part agrees to.

modalities.name: Common Cause Steps
modalities.tagline: Find the value hiding in each part's objection, then act on it.
modalities.whatItIs: Common Cause Steps is a proposed approach for times when an inner part objects to a step you value. Instead of overruling the part, you ask what it cares about, since a part's fear often points to a value of its own, such as a critic that cares about good work or a worrier that cares about the people you love. The step is then reshaped to serve both your value and the part's, while the fear itself is allowed to stay.
modalities.coreIdea: A part that resists a valued step is often guarding something that matters too, so its fear can show what else is at stake. Steps that honor both values may feel less like a fight, even when the fear comes along.
modalities.whatYouDo: In weekly 50-minute sessions with a therapist trained in both acceptance-based and parts work, you choose a value and a concrete step, such as applying for a new job, then notice which part objects and where you feel it in the body. You ask that part what it fears would happen and what it is trying to look after, write its value beside yours on a card, and reshape the step so it serves both, for example asking a friend to read your application first out of respect for the critic's care for good work. You take the step during the week, letting the fear be there, and review in the next session which value each part held and how the step went.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who know what matters to them but keep meeting the same inner objections, and who want to understand those objections rather than push past them. It suits people looking for present-focused work rather than deep trauma work.
modalities.cautions: An untested concept: turning toward parts can stir strong feelings, so the therapist should be ready to pause the step if a part is very distressed. It is not a substitute for tested care for severe depression, suicidal thoughts or serious substance problems.
modalities.tweet: What if your inner critic cares about something too? Common Cause Steps is a proposed practice: when a part of you objects to a valued step, ask what it's trying to look after, then shape the step to honor its value and yours. The fear can come along.

modalities.name: Reading the Old Truce
modalities.tagline: Put both sides of a stubborn habit into words, then reread them.
modalities.whatItIs: Reading the Old Truce is a new concept for experiential therapy built on the idea that a stubborn symptom can be the settlement between two opposite emotional demands, each learned long ago. Last-minute rushing, for example, might settle a clash between a side that insists your work must never be judged and a side that refuses to be told what to do, since leaving everything late gives each side something. It works only with memories you already have, treats images and feelings as experiences rather than evidence of what happened, and is never used to uncover forgotten events.
modalities.coreIdea: A symptom that seems senseless may make sense as an old truce whose terms have never been said aloud. Putting each side's demand into plain words and rereading the whole truce often, without arguing with it, may let terms that no longer fit lose their hold, and the symptom with them.
modalities.whatYouDo: Over about 8 to 12 sessions, a licensed clinician trained in trauma care helps you find the two sides of a symptom and put each side's demand into one first-person sentence, reworded until it feels true, such as 'nobody ever gets to judge my work' and 'nobody tells me what to do'. The clinician writes both sentences on one card, with the symptom as the settlement between them, and you read the card aloud once a day without trying to change anything, noting which lines still feel true. In each session you go over those notes together, recall what you already remember about when each demand began, and notice whether the symptom shifts as any line starts to sound out of date.
modalities.whoItsFor: People with a symptom or habit that keeps returning however hard they fight it, and who sense two sides of themselves pulling in opposite directions. It suits those open to emotionally vivid sessions.
modalities.cautions: Untried and intense: putting old demands into words can bring up strong feelings or memories, which is why a licensed clinician trained in trauma care leads every session, and people with severe trauma, dissociation or a current crisis should get stabilizing care first. Medical causes of a symptom should be ruled out first, and it should not replace well-tested care for conditions such as ADHD, PTSD or major depression.
modalities.tweet: Always rushing at the last minute? It might be an old truce: one side of you insists your work must never be judged, another refuses to be told what to do. Reading the Old Truce is an untested therapy idea: put both sides into words, then reread them daily.

modalities.name: Ask the Tight Spot
modalities.tagline: Ask your body's guarding first, then let shaking through if it agrees.
modalities.whatItIs: Ask the Tight Spot is an experimental body practice that regards stubborn tension as a protective part with its own reasons. Before letting mild tremors run through the body, you turn toward the area that braces, ask what it is guarding against, and ask whether it is willing to let a little shaking through. It never goes looking for forgotten events: it works only with what you already remember, and any image or feeling that comes up is treated as part of the exercise, not as evidence of the past.
modalities.coreIdea: A clenched jaw or tight belly may be guarding something, and forcing it to let go can make it grip harder. Asking the bracing area for permission, and respecting a no, aims to make release feel safer and more willing.
modalities.whatYouDo: You learn it over four to six sessions with a clinician who is a trained tremoring (TRE) provider, familiar with parts work, and who first screens your physical and mental health: a few leg-tiring stretches, then lying on your back with knees bent. Before tremors start, you notice where the body braces, get curious about it as you would about a part, and ask whether it is okay to let some shaking through; if the answer feels like yes, you let gentle tremors run for a few minutes at most, ending the round at any moment by straightening your legs or rolling onto your side, and if it feels like no, you rest and thank it. Home practice of 20 to 30 minutes comes only after that, with regular check-ins with the same clinician.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who hold tension in particular spots and want a body-based practice that respects their own pace. It may suit those who find parts work too wordy, or forced release too much.
modalities.cautions: Untested: tremoring and parts work can each bring up strong emotions or memories, so people with severe trauma, dissociation, psychosis or bipolar disorder should learn it only with a clinically trained provider, and anyone with epilepsy or seizures, pregnancy, recent surgery, fractures or other injuries should check with a doctor first. Stop whenever you feel overwhelmed, numb or in pain, and keep up any other care you have.
modalities.tweet: Body-based idea: Ask the Tight Spot. Before letting your body shake out tension, you turn to the tight spot (jaw, shoulders, belly), ask what it's guarding, and only let tremors through if it seems willing. Release that respects your body's no.

modalities.name: Both Pulls at Once
modalities.tagline: Sense both sides of a dilemma as one knot in the body.
modalities.whatItIs: Both Pulls at Once is a new concept for inner conflict, for the times when part of you wants one thing and part of you wants another. Instead of talking with each side in turn, you sense the whole conflict as a single felt knot in the body, find a word or image for it, and wait for it to loosen in its own way. Nothing here is meant to uncover forgotten events: only memories you already hold are used, and pictures or feelings that arise are not proof of what really happened.
modalities.coreIdea: Two sides of a conflict may share one bodily feel, and that felt whole may hold an answer neither side can say alone. Staying gently with the knot, rather than siding with either part, leaves room for a small felt shift that includes both.
modalities.whatYouDo: The first sessions, 30 to 45 minutes each, are with a therapist trained in Focusing and parts work: you briefly name the two sides of a dilemma, then ask how the whole thing feels in your body, for example a pull in the chest against a heaviness in the belly. You find a handle for the knot, such as "tight rope", check that it fits, and ask it open questions like "what does this need?" while the therapist mostly just reflects back your words. Later you can practice with a trained listening partner, with the therapist available to talk.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel torn, such as between staying and leaving, and are tired of arguing with themselves. It suits those who like quiet, body-aware exploration and can practice in pairs.
modalities.cautions: An untested idea: staying with inner conflict can bring up strong feelings or old memories, and some people find the felt sense hard to notice at first. People with severe trauma, dissociation or a current crisis should practice with a qualified therapist rather than a peer.
modalities.tweet: Torn between two choices? Here's a novel idea: Both Pulls at Once. Instead of arguing with yourself, you feel the whole conflict as one knot in your body, give it a name, and gently wait to see whether it loosens. Quiet, body-aware, begun with a therapist.

modalities.name: Growing Up Slowly
modalities.tagline: Let a young inner part grow up in its own time.
modalities.whatItIs: Growing Up Slowly is a proposed coaching practice built on the idea that a part formed in childhood can stay the age it was when it formed, and might keep growing if it is simply kept company. Instead of releasing what a part carries, or showing it anything, you return to the same young part every few weeks and notice, without pushing, whether it has started to look, sound or feel older. Only memories you already have are used, vivid images and feelings are not taken as evidence of what happened, and the practice is never used to uncover forgotten events.
modalities.coreIdea: A frightened seven-year-old part may stay seven because nobody stayed with it long enough for it to grow. Patient, unhurried company over many months, rather than a technique, may let it ripen into an older and steadier version of itself.
modalities.whatYouDo: Every three weeks or so, over about a year, you meet a coach or therapist trained in parts work for an hour and check in with the same young part, noticing how old it seems today and how it holds itself, sometimes sketching it in a notebook. The guide never asks the part to grow and simply helps you stay with it warmly; across months, the sketches and notes form a timeline of any changes. Between sessions you just notice the part in daily life, without exercises.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who keep meeting the same young, scared or angry part of themselves and want a slow, gentle way to stay with it. It suits those not in crisis who prefer patience to techniques.
modalities.cautions: Untested, and coaching rather than therapy: staying with a young part can bring up old trauma, so choose a coach trained in parts work who knows when to refer you to a therapist, or work with a therapist instead. People with severe depression, PTSD, dissociation, psychosis or suicidal thoughts should work with a licensed mental health professional.
modalities.tweet: Ever notice a part of you that still feels about seven years old? Growing Up Slowly is a coaching concept: return to that young part every few weeks, keep it warm company, never push, and see whether it starts to grow up in its own time. Slow by design.

modalities.name: The Manager's Day Off
modalities.tagline: Open sitting where every urge to steer is greeted, then rested.
modalities.whatItIs: The Manager's Day Off is a playful, untested twist on open, objectless meditation. Whenever you catch an urge to control your attention (to focus harder, change a feeling or meditate well), you recognize it as a managing part trying to help, briefly thank it and offer it the rest of the sit off.
modalities.coreIdea: The effort to control experience may be the work of a hard-working inner manager, and simply dropping that effort can feel like ignoring it. Greeting the manager kindly, then letting it rest, may make letting go feel safe rather than like a fight.
modalities.whatYouDo: A therapist familiar with parts work and meditation introduces it in one or two sessions and records a short guide. At home you then sit comfortably for 15 to 30 minutes, eyes open or closed, with no chosen focus, and each time you notice an intention to steer, you silently say something like "I see you, thanks, you can rest" and do nothing further, not even returning to a focus. The therapist stays available to talk about anything difficult that comes up.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are always managing, planning or monitoring, and who find that meditation turns into one more task. It may appeal to people who already know their inner managers from parts work.
modalities.cautions: An untested idea: with no anchor you may drift into worry or doze, and letting managers rest can sometimes uncover the feelings they were guarding, so keep sits short at first. People with significant trauma, psychosis or dissociation should go slowly with the therapist's support and avoid intensive retreats.
modalities.tweet: Prototype for over-thinkers: The Manager's Day Off. Sit with no focus. Each time you catch yourself trying to control your attention, greet that inner manager, thank it, and give it the afternoon off. Meditation for people who turn everything into a task.

modalities.name: The Part They Stir
modalities.tagline: Wish each person well, then the part of you they stir.
modalities.whatItIs: The Part They Stir is a proposed loving-kindness meditation that runs two circles at once: the usual widening circle of people, and the parts of you that each person sets off. When you wish a difficult colleague well and something in you bristles, you turn to that bristling part, offer it the same kind wishes, then go back to the colleague.
modalities.coreIdea: Goodwill toward a difficult person may stall because a protective part of you objects, and pushing past it can make the wishes hollow. Including that part in the circle, rather than overriding it, may let goodwill toward the person grow on firmer ground.
modalities.whatYouDo: You learn it over about four sessions with a therapist trained in parts work who also teaches meditation, then practice daily at home with a recording and check in every few weeks. In each 20 to 30 minute sit you offer phrases such as "may you be safe, may you be at ease" to a loved one, a neutral person and then someone difficult, and whenever a part of you reacts (a guarded one, a hurt one, a resentful one), you offer it the same phrases before returning to the person. You save the most difficult people for days when the warmth feels steady.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find that loving-kindness practice stalls or feels fake when they reach someone difficult. It may suit those who already know their protective parts and want a gentle, structured daily practice.
modalities.cautions: Untested: turning toward difficult people and the parts they stir can bring up grief, anger or old hurt, so start with mildly difficult people and keep sessions short. If parts linked to trauma come up strongly, stop and bring them to the therapist, and anyone with a history of psychosis or dissociation should talk to a clinician before starting.
modalities.tweet: Ever try to wish someone well and feel part of you bristle? The Part They Stir is a new idea for loving-kindness meditation: wish them well, then offer the same kindness to the part of you they set off, then go back to them. 💛

modalities.name: Just Passing Through
modalities.tagline: Note each inner part as it arrives and leaves, like a visitor.
modalities.whatItIs: Just Passing Through is a new concept that brings the close, moment-by-moment noting of insight meditation to the parts of your mind. Besides noting sensations, you note which part has arrived (the planner, the worrier, the critic), watch it stay a while and notice when it leaves, as you would a visitor. It does not dig for forgotten events, it stays with memories you already have, and whatever images or feelings arise are not treated as evidence about the past.
modalities.coreIdea: When a part takes over, it can feel like who you are, but parts may come and go like visitors through a house. Noting their arrivals and departures, again and again, may show that none of them is the one doing the noticing, which could make even strong parts easier to be with.
modalities.whatYouDo: It is taught over a few sessions by a meditation teacher working alongside a therapist trained in parts work, then practiced at home a few times a week with regular check-ins. In a 30-minute sitting you rest attention on the breath and body, and whenever a part shows up you note it softly, such as "worrier arriving", then note how it shows up in the body and when it leaves ("worrier gone"). Over weeks you may notice which visitors come most often, how long they stay and what was here before they came.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who get swept away by strong inner states, such as anxiety or self-criticism, and want a structured way to meet them in meditation. It suits those with some sitting experience.
modalities.cautions: No one has studied this combination: watching intense parts closely can sometimes bring up fear, panic or old memories, so start with milder ones and keep the therapist's support. People with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should talk to a clinician first and avoid intensive retreats.
modalities.tweet: Meditation idea for anyone whose inner critic or worrier takes over: Just Passing Through. Sit quietly and note each part as it arrives ('worrier here'), stays a while and leaves ('worrier gone'). The hope: they start to feel like visitors, not like you.

modalities.name: Breathless Curiosity
modalities.tagline: Practice getting curious about your inner parts while still out of breath.
modalities.whatItIs: Breathless Curiosity is a proposed interval workout that uses hard efforts to bring inner parts into view, such as the one that pushes past every limit, the one that compares you with others and the one that wants out. In each recovery period, still breathing fast, you notice which part spoke during the effort and practice stepping back from it with curiosity. The past enters only through memories you already have; imagery and feelings are never treated as evidence of what happened, and the practice is never used to uncover forgotten events.
modalities.coreIdea: Stepping back from a part is usually practiced in calm, but life's hardest moments come with a racing heart. Practicing curiosity in the activated minutes after a hard bout aims to make that skill available when it is most needed.
modalities.whatYouDo: A therapist trained in parts work meets you for a first session to practice naming parts and stepping back, and a coach sets up the intervals. Then, two or three times a week, after a 10-minute warm-up on a bike, rower or brisk incline walk, you do 6 to 8 bouts of 1 to 2 minutes at a hard but controlled effort with 2 to 3 minutes of easy movement between, and in each recovery you silently name the loudest part, ask what it is worried about and choose your next effort from a calmer place, which can mean easing off. You bring what you notice to occasional check-ins with the therapist.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who already enjoy hard exercise and notice harsh inner voices while doing it, and those who want to practice staying curious under stress. It suits people who prefer active practice to sitting still.
modalities.cautions: An untested concept: hard bouts strain the heart, so check with a doctor before starting (especially with heart problems, fainting or high blood pressure), always warm up, build up gradually, keep easy days between sessions and stop at once for chest pain, dizziness, faintness, unusual breathlessness or pain. Turning toward parts while highly activated can also stir intense memories or a backlash from protective parts, so if that happens, stop the inner work and talk it through with the therapist, and people with trauma or dissociation should start more gently.
modalities.tweet: 'Push harder.' 'Everyone's faster than you.' Hear those mid-workout? Breathless Curiosity is a new concept: interval training where, in each recovery minute, you name the part that spoke and get curious about it. Practice staying steady when your heart races.
